title: Nawras owners pitch (English)
note: One entry per slide, in slide order; ids are the deck data-ids.

slides.title: Nawras: Fusha for little hearts, by the Pacific
slides.transcript: [warmly] Assalamu alaikum. In ten minutes I will show you what we built for your school, under one name: Nawras. At the end I will ask you for five decisions: which look, which logo, which class tries it first, which teacher checks the Fusha, and how many books to print. Let us start with the children.

slides.title: Fusha has our hours: one lesson, four ways
slides.transcript: Our students live in English, and at home in a dialect. Fusha, the language of the Qur'an, gets only the hours they spend with us. So those hours must be joyful. Let me ask you, as parents: when your own child comes to Arabic class, do they run in, or drag their feet? Here is our idea. We write a lesson once, carefully, in correct Fusha. The child gets it four ways: on a screen at home, on the classroom television with the teacher, in a printed book they write in, and read aloud in their ears. Teachers teach; Nawras makes it joyful.

slides.title: The Nawras website, live
slides.transcript: This is the website itself, the real homepage, not a picture. Scroll inside the frame and look around. Parents see Noori, the colours, and Arabic words with an English line underneath. And they see one thing to do: Book a free trial class. Press the button to open it in its own tab, then try it on your own phone.

slides.title: The name: the seagull and Noori
slides.transcript: The name is Nawras, the seagull. Children in San Diego see seagulls every time they go to the beach. A seagull flies far and always comes home, like our children returning to the language of the Qur'an. Our mascot is a young seagull called Noori, from nur, light. He is round and kind, never scary. If you prefer another name, we prepared four more; they are at the bottom of the slide.

slides.title: Six logo ideas, one recommended
slides.transcript: We drew six logo ideas, and you can try them yourselves: tap a number. None of the drawings has letters in it; the name is set in real Arabic type underneath. Switch the background to see it on light and on dark. Our recommendation is number one, the Gull and Crescent: the crescent says Islamic, the wave says San Diego, and Noori says children. For small places, like a phone icon, we pair it with number six, Noori's face. The tiny one shows how it looks on a phone.

slides.title: Six layouts and six themes
slides.transcript: Now the look of the website. There are six layouts and six colour themes, and they mix. Choose a layout in the top row, then a theme in the second row, and watch the page change. Andalus is a garden arch, Pacific is the ocean and the most playful, Fanous is lanterns at night, Kurrasa is a school notebook, Mosaic is bold tiles and stars, and Mihrab is soft and quiet. Which one feels like your school? You do not have to answer now; I will ask again at the end.

slides.title: One lesson, three ways
slides.transcript: To show the format, we built one real lesson for grades one and two: hadha and hadhihi, "this" for masculine and for feminine words. The little ta marbuta becomes a seashell that Noori finds on the beach. The lesson comes three ways. An article to read together, about fifteen minutes, with five questions and a worksheet. A story with Noori and his friends Sami and Salma, read aloud in Fusha or Egyptian. And slides for the teacher, eighteen of them in about twenty minutes, with games. Tap a card to open any of them.

slides.title: Writing on the screen
slides.transcript: Tapping is not enough; children must write. On an iPad the child traces the shell letter, then hadhihi, with a finger or an Apple Pencil, from the green dot, right to left. The buttons are big: colours, eraser, undo, clear. When they press "I finished", they get a star. We never grade handwriting automatically and never mark it wrong; that judgement stays with the teacher.

slides.title: The 32-page printed book
slides.transcript: Now off the screen and into their hands. This is the book: Noori and the Little Shell. Thirty-two pages, square, in full colour, printed on demand by Lulu. Fourteen story pages, eleven exercise pages, a certificate, and an answer page for parents. On every exercise page there is a Q R code; a parent scans it and the book opens on the web, read aloud in Fusha or in Egyptian. Scan this one now, or press a button to hear. The buttons below open the real print files: the book, the cover, a booklet to print at home, and the worksheets.

slides.title: Islamic adab, and what Nawras is not
slides.transcript: You care about adab, and so do we. These rules are written into everything we make. No pictures of prophets or angels. No verses of the Qur'an as decoration or inside a game. Modest clothing on every child; when a picture came out wrong, we drew it again. No music, only soft sounds. And a word about what Nawras is not. It does not replace your teachers: the teacher presents and judges the writing. It is not an app, and families pay no subscription. And today it is one lesson that shows the format, not a full curriculum.

slides.title: The five steps of every new lesson
slides.transcript: How does this grow beyond one lesson? Every new lesson follows the same five steps. We write it once, every word in Fusha. We draw the pictures on our own computer, so Noori always looks like himself. We build the web book and the slides from that text. The print files and Q R codes are made and checked automatically. And the narration is recorded and checked word by word. Right now we are drawing a fuller set of colour pictures, and the next step is a short guide for pictures and animation.

slides.title: Five decisions
slides.transcript: So here are the five decisions. One: the look, one of the six; the choice is yours. Two: the logo; we recommend the Gull and Crescent, with Noori's face as the icon. Three: a pilot class, which grade and which teacher, and from when; let us fill that in together. Four: one teacher who proofreads the Fusha, every vowel mark, before anything is printed. This one matters most, because children copy exactly what they see. Five: a printing budget. A Lulu paperback is about eight to fifteen dollars a copy, so a class of twenty is about one hundred and sixty to three hundred dollars; these are October estimates. We print one proof copy first, which takes five to ten days. The website costs nothing extra, and a home booklet costs one to three dollars. Which of these can we decide today?

slides.title: What your school has now
slides.transcript: [warmly] Here is what your school has today: a name, a look, a logo, one lesson in three forms, and a book with its own voice. One lesson, written once in careful Fusha, reaching each child on a screen, in class, on paper and in their ears. With your five decisions, it reaches your students next. May Allah bless your school, your teachers and your children.
